questions.stem: The Bronze Age is named after an alloy that early metalworkers made by melting together two metals obtained from ores. Which two metals?
options: Iron and carbon
Lead and zinc
Gold and silver
Copper and tin
questions.explanation: Bronze is an alloy of copper with a small amount of tin, which is harder than copper alone. Iron with a little carbon makes steel, a later technology of the Iron Age.

questions.stem: Roman builders made a durable concrete by mixing lime with volcanic ash. Which statement best describes the geological resources used?
options: Lime from heated limestone and ash from volcanic deposits
Lime from crushed granite and ash from burnt coal seams
Lime from evaporated seawater and ash from burnt timber in kilns
Lime from heated sandstone and ash from weathered basalt
questions.explanation: Lime is made by heating limestone (calcium carbonate) to drive off carbon dioxide. The Romans mixed it with volcanic ash, which reacts with lime and water to set hard. Granite and sandstone contain little calcium carbonate, so they cannot be burnt to lime.

questions.stem: A person in a wealthy city and a person in a remote farming village each list the geological resources they use in a day. Which difference is most likely?
options: The city dweller uses far more metals, fuels and building materials per person
The village dweller uses more metals, because all of the farm tools and fences are made of steel
Both use similar amounts, because everyone needs the same basic resources
The city dweller uses fewer resources, because city flats are smaller
questions.explanation: Industrialised lifestyles depend on large amounts of steel, concrete, copper wiring, electronics and fuel for transport and electricity, so use per person is much higher. A few steel tools in a village are small compared with a city's infrastructure, cars and appliances.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-metallic geological resource?
options: Chalcopyrite used as a source of copper
Phosphate rock used to make fertiliser
Bauxite used to make aluminium metal
Galena used as a source of lead
questions.explanation: Phosphate rock is mined for its phosphorus, which goes into fertiliser, not for a metal. Bauxite, galena and chalcopyrite are ores mined to extract aluminium, lead and copper.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a mineral resource and a mineral reserve?
options: A resource is the part of a reserve that has already been mined out
A reserve is any deposit found by drilling, whatever its grade or depth
A resource is a deposit that can be mined at a profit with current methods
A reserve is the part of a resource that can be mined at a profit now
questions.explanation: A resource is the whole identified concentration of a material that could one day be extracted. The reserve is the smaller part that can be extracted economically with today's technology and prices, so it changes as prices and methods change.

questions.stem: A country has 600 million tonnes of a mineral in reserve and mines 20 million tonnes a year. If production stays the same, how long will the reserve last?
options: 12 years
300 years
580 years
30 years
questions.explanation: Reserve life is the reserve divided by the annual rate of use: 600 / 20 = 30 years. Subtracting one year's production from the reserve gives 580, which is not a time.

questions.stem: A metal's reserve life was estimated at 30 years in one decade, yet 30 years later the estimate was still about 30 years, although mining continued. Which explanation is best supported?
options: The metal re-formed in the ground at about the same rate as it was being mined
The original estimate counted the whole resource rather than only the mineable reserve
Recycling returned all the mined metal to the ground, so the reserve was refilled
New discoveries, better technology and higher prices turned resources into reserves
questions.explanation: Reserves are economic estimates. Exploration finds new deposits, and better technology or higher prices make lower-grade ore profitable, so reserves can grow while mining continues. Ore deposits form over geological time, so they do not re-form within decades.

questions.stem: The idea of 'peak oil' is based on the observation that oil production from a region tends to follow a bell-shaped curve. What does the model predict?
options: Production rises steadily until the last barrel is pumped, then stops suddenly
Production stays constant until about half the oil is gone, then doubles
Production falls at first, then rises as new technology reaches the field
Production rises, reaches a maximum and then declines as fields deplete
questions.explanation: In the peak oil model, production rises as fields are found and developed, reaches a peak, then declines as the easiest oil is used and discoveries fall. A sudden stop at full production is the common misconception the model replaced.

questions.stem: Why are coal, petroleum and metallic ores classed as non-renewable resources?
options: They form over geological time, far more slowly than they are used
They cannot be recycled once they are mined and used
They are found only in small amounts within the Earth
They form only at ancient plate boundaries, which are now all inactive
questions.explanation: These resources take millions of years to form, so on a human time-scale they are not replenished. Metals can in fact be recycled, and many fuels and ores occur in large amounts, so neither of those makes them non-renewable.

questions.stem: Global use of a non-metallic resource, construction sand, is rising fast. Desert sand is abundant, yet builders rarely use it. Why does this not make sand use sustainable?
options: Desert sand contains too little silica to be used in glass or in concrete
Desert sand is a renewable resource, so using it would not count as mining
Desert sand is too coarse and angular to mix evenly into a concrete batch
Wind-rounded desert grains bind poorly in concrete, so river and marine sand is used up
questions.explanation: Wind abrasion makes desert grains small and well rounded, so they interlock poorly and make weak concrete. Builders rely on angular river, lake and marine sand, which is being extracted faster than it is replaced. Desert sand is mostly quartz, so lack of silica is not the reason.

questions.stem: From which material does coal mainly form?
options: Land plants that accumulated in swamps
Marine plankton buried on the sea floor
Shells of marine animals on reefs
Animal remains buried in desert sand
questions.explanation: Coal forms from thick layers of land plant material in swamps and peat bogs. Marine plankton is the main source of petroleum, and shells form limestone.

questions.stem: Why must swamp plants be covered by water and sediment soon after they die for coal to form?
options: Low-oxygen conditions slow decay, so the carbon-rich material is kept
The water dissolves the plant cellulose and leaves only the carbon behind
The sediment supplies the carbon that turns the plants into coal
The water cools the plants so they freeze before they can decay
questions.explanation: Waterlogged, oxygen-poor conditions slow the bacteria and fungi that would otherwise decompose the plants, so the organic matter builds up as peat. Burial then compacts and heats it. The carbon comes from the plants, not the sediment.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows increasing rank of coal?
options: Peat, anthracite, lignite, bituminous coal
Peat, lignite, bituminous coal, anthracite
Lignite, peat, anthracite, bituminous coal
Anthracite, bituminous coal, lignite, peat
questions.explanation: With deeper burial, heat and pressure turn peat into lignite (brown coal), then bituminous (black) coal, then anthracite. The reverse order lists falling rank.

questions.stem: As coal increases in rank from lignite to anthracite, how do its carbon and moisture contents change?
options: Both carbon and moisture contents rise
Both carbon and moisture contents fall
Carbon content rises and moisture content falls
Carbon content falls and moisture content rises
questions.explanation: Heat and pressure drive off water and volatile compounds, so higher-rank coal holds a higher proportion of carbon and releases more energy per kilogram. Lignite is the wettest and lowest in carbon.

questions.stem: Seam X is soft, brown and crumbly, with visible plant fragments. Seam Y is hard, black and shiny. Both formed from similar plants. Which inference is best supported?
options: X formed from older plants, so more of its carbon has been lost over time
Y formed in a drier swamp, so less water was trapped among its plant remains
X was heated more strongly, so its plant fragments were preserved by the baking
Y was buried more deeply or for longer, so it reached higher heat and pressure
questions.explanation: Seam X has the features of lignite and seam Y those of bituminous coal or anthracite. Higher rank comes from greater burial depth, heat and time, which drive off water and volatiles. Strong heating destroys plant structure, so it does not preserve it.

questions.stem: Petroleum forms mainly from which material?
options: Microscopic marine plankton and algae
Woody remains of large land plants
Limestone formed from coral reefs
Volcanic gases trapped in sediment
questions.explanation: Plankton and algae settle with fine mud on oxygen-poor sea or lake floors. Burial converts them to kerogen and then to oil and gas. Woody land plants mainly form coal.

questions.stem: Kerogen in a buried source rock produces oil only within a range of temperatures called the oil window. What happens if the rock is buried deeper and heated further?
options: The oil breaks down into natural gas
The oil changes back into kerogen
The oil hardens into anthracite coal
The oil is oxidised to carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: At higher temperatures the large oil molecules crack into smaller ones, so deeper, hotter source rocks yield mainly gas. The change cannot reverse to kerogen, and anthracite forms from plant material, not oil.

questions.stem: Why does oil formed in a source rock migrate upwards into other rocks?
options: It is drawn upwards by the heat escaping from the mantle
It is pushed up by plants absorbing water at the surface
It is more dense than the rock grains that surround it
It is less dense than the water filling the pore spaces
questions.explanation: Oil and gas are less dense than groundwater, so they rise through permeable rock until an impermeable layer stops them. Without a seal they would reach the surface and escape.

questions.stem: How is coal-seam gas formed and held in the ground?
options: Methane forms from volcanic gases and dissolves in groundwater below the coal
Methane forms in swamps at the surface and is sealed in as the peat is buried
Methane forms as coal matures and sticks to the coal's surfaces under water pressure
Methane forms from plankton in marine shale and migrates up into a sandstone reservoir rock
questions.explanation: Coal-seam gas is mostly methane produced by microbes and by heating as coal matures. It is adsorbed onto the internal surfaces of the coal and held there by the pressure of water in the seam. Gas that forms from plankton and migrates into sandstone is conventional natural gas.

questions.stem: A petroleum trap needs a reservoir rock and a cap rock. Which pair fits these roles?
options: Porous sandstone as the reservoir; shale as the cap rock
Shale as the reservoir; porous sandstone as the cap rock
Granite as the reservoir; porous limestone as the cap rock
Coal as the reservoir; fractured sandstone as the cap rock
questions.explanation: A reservoir rock must be porous and permeable to store and yield oil, as many sandstones are. A cap rock must be impermeable, as shale and salt are. Swapping them would let the oil escape.

questions.stem: In an anticline trap, oil, gas and water have separated in the reservoir rock. In what order are they found from top to bottom?
options: Oil, then gas, then water
Water, then oil, then gas
Gas, then water, then oil
Gas, then oil, then water
questions.explanation: The fluids separate by density. Gas is the least dense so it gathers at the crest of the fold, oil lies below it, and water fills the pores beneath.

questions.stem: A seismic profile shows rock layers arched upwards into a dome, with a shale layer over a porous sandstone. Why is the crest of the arch a target for drilling?
options: The heat at the crest of the fold turns the sandstone itself into petroleum
The crest is where the shale is thinnest, so oil passes most easily into the well
Oil sinks through the shale and pools in the lowest part of the sandstone
Oil and gas rising through the sandstone collect beneath the shale at the crest
questions.explanation: This is an anticline trap. Buoyant oil and gas move up through the permeable sandstone and collect at the highest point, where the impermeable shale stops them. They rise, not sink.

questions.stem: A geologist finds a porous sandstone that thins and ends against impermeable shale, with no folding or faulting. Oil is found where the sandstone pinches out. What type of trap is this?
options: A stratigraphic trap
An anticline trap
A fault trap
A salt dome trap
questions.explanation: In a stratigraphic trap the seal comes from a change in rock type within the sequence, such as a sandstone pinching out into shale. Anticline, fault and salt dome traps all need the rocks to be deformed, which the scenario rules out.

questions.stem: How can a fault form a petroleum trap?
options: Movement opens a gap that lets oil drain down into the lower layers
Movement heats the rock along the fault and turns kerogen into oil
Movement crushes the reservoir rock so that it becomes far more porous and permeable
Movement places an impermeable layer against the end of a porous reservoir
questions.explanation: When rocks are displaced along a fault, the end of a sloping reservoir rock can come to rest against shale or another impermeable layer, which seals it. A fault that opens a pathway lets oil escape instead of trapping it.

questions.stem: A layer of rock salt has risen as a plug through overlying sedimentary rocks. Why do salt domes form petroleum traps?
options: Salt is porous and permeable, so the oil collects in the salt itself
Salt reacts with kerogen to produce oil in the rocks around the dome
Salt is denser than the rocks around it, so it drags the oil down beside the dome
Salt is impermeable and bends up the rocks beside it, sealing their reservoirs
questions.explanation: Salt is less dense than the surrounding rocks, so it rises and bends up the layers it pierces. It is also impermeable, so oil moving up a tilted reservoir is sealed against the salt. Salt is neither a reservoir nor denser than sediment.

questions.stem: In a large body of mafic magma, chromite crystallises early and forms layers on the floor of the magma chamber. What process concentrates the chromite?
options: Rivers sorting chromite grains by their density
Deep weathering removing the soluble minerals
Gravity settling of dense crystals through the melt
Hot fluids depositing chromite in fractured rock
questions.explanation: Chromite is denser than the surrounding melt, so crystals that form early sink and pile up as layers on the chamber floor. Hydrothermal veins, river placers and weathering residues are other concentration processes that act outside a magma chamber.

questions.stem: How do hydrothermal vein deposits form?
options: Hot, metal-rich water cools in rock fractures and minerals precipitate
Molten metal flows into cracks and sets solid as the rock around it cools
Rainwater dissolves metals at the surface and deposits them in rivers
Dense crystals sink through magma and settle into cracks in its floor
questions.explanation: Hot water, often released from cooling magma, dissolves metals. As it rises through fractures it cools and loses pressure, so ore minerals such as galena, sphalerite, chalcopyrite and gold precipitate with quartz in veins.

questions.stem: Gold-bearing quartz veins cut through rocks around a granite intrusion. Which observation best supports a hydrothermal origin?
options: The gold lies in a layer on the floor of the granite intrusion
The veins are found only in the soil profile above the granite
The veins fill fractures and contain minerals that crystallise from hot water
The gold forms rounded grains mixed with river pebbles in the veins
questions.explanation: Veins filling fractures, with quartz that grew from solution, show minerals were deposited from circulating hot fluids. Rounded gold among pebbles describes a placer, and a layer on a magma chamber floor describes gravity settling.

questions.stem: Gold eroded from a quartz vein is carried downstream. Where in a river is placer gold most likely to collect?
options: On the inside of a bend where the water slows
On the outside of a bend where the water is fastest
In fine mud on the floodplain far from the channel
In the fastest-flowing water in mid-channel rapids
questions.explanation: Gold is very dense, so it drops out wherever the current slows, such as inside bends and behind bars and rock ledges. Fast water keeps lighter grains moving, leaving gold concentrated with other heavy minerals.

questions.stem: Placer deposits contain gold, rutile and zircon but almost no feldspar or mica, although all of these were in the source rocks. Which property explains this?
options: The placer minerals are soft, so they are ground into fine sand
The placer minerals dissolve in water and then recrystallise
The placer minerals are magnetic, so they cling to the riverbed
The placer minerals are dense and resist weathering and abrasion
questions.explanation: Minerals concentrated in placers must survive transport and settle out quickly, so they are dense and chemically and physically resistant. Feldspar and mica weather to clay and are light, so they are carried away. Rutile and zircon are not magnetic.

questions.stem: Bauxite forms by deep weathering of rocks in a hot, wet climate. How does weathering concentrate the aluminium?
options: Rainwater leaches away soluble elements, leaving aluminium hydroxides behind
Rainwater dissolves the aluminium and redeposits it in the nearby river gravels
Heat from the tropical climate melts the rock and separates the aluminium
Plants take up aluminium from the soil and concentrate it in leaf litter
questions.explanation: Intense chemical weathering removes silica and soluble cations such as sodium, potassium and calcium, leaving a residue rich in insoluble aluminium hydroxides. This is a residual deposit, not a placer.

questions.stem: Above a copper sulfide ore body, surface rock is a rusty iron oxide cap. Below it is barren leached rock, then a rich copper zone at the water table above unweathered ore. Which process formed the rich zone?
options: Gravity settling: dense copper sulfides sank to the base of a magma chamber
Placer formation: copper grains were washed downhill and sorted by a stream
Hydrothermal intrusion: a later magma body injected new copper at the water table
Supergene enrichment: copper leached above was redeposited at the water table
questions.explanation: Oxidising groundwater dissolves copper from sulfides near the surface and carries it down. Below the water table conditions are reducing, so copper minerals precipitate and enrich that zone. The rusty iron oxide cap left behind is a gossan.

questions.stem: Banded iron formations have alternating layers of iron oxides and chert. Why could large amounts of dissolved iron build up in the early oceans before they formed?
options: The oceans were much less salty, so dissolved iron could not combine with any oxygen
The atmosphere and oceans had little free oxygen, so iron stayed dissolved
The oceans were far hotter, so iron oxides could dissolve in seawater
Volcanoes released oxygen that kept the iron dissolved in seawater
questions.explanation: In an anaerobic environment, iron stays in its soluble reduced form (Fe2+). Once oxygen became available it oxidised the iron to insoluble Fe3+ oxides, which settled to the sea floor. Volcanoes mainly released water vapour and carbon dioxide, not oxygen.

questions.stem: Which sequence best explains the formation of banded iron formations?
options: Dissolved iron oxidises, photosynthesisers release oxygen, iron is dissolved
Photosynthesisers release oxygen, dissolved iron oxidises, iron oxides settle
Iron oxides settle, photosynthesisers release oxygen, dissolved iron forms
Volcanoes release oxygen, iron oxides dissolve, photosynthesisers use iron
questions.explanation: Oxygen produced by photosynthesising cyanobacteria reacted with dissolved iron, forming insoluble iron oxides such as haematite and magnetite that settled as layers. The other orders put the effect before its cause.

questions.stem: A heavy, metallic grey mineral breaks into perfect cubes along its cleavage planes and leaves a grey streak. It is a major ore of lead. Which mineral is it?
options: Magnetite
Haematite
Graphite
Galena
questions.explanation: Galena (lead sulfide, PbS) is dense, silvery grey and has cubic cleavage. Magnetite is black and magnetic, haematite gives a red-brown streak, and graphite is very soft and greasy with a black streak.

questions.stem: Two black iron ore samples look alike. Sample 1 is attracted to a hand magnet and gives a black streak. Sample 2 is not magnetic and gives a red-brown streak. Which identification is correct?
options: 1 is haematite and 2 is magnetite
1 is chalcopyrite and 2 is galena
1 is galena and 2 is chalcopyrite
1 is magnetite and 2 is haematite
questions.explanation: Magnetite (Fe3O4) is strongly magnetic and has a black streak. Haematite (Fe2O3) can be black or steel grey in hand specimen, but its streak is always red-brown, which makes streak the reliable test.

questions.stem: A brassy yellow mineral is mistaken for gold. It gives a greenish-black streak and is scratched by a steel knife. Which mineral is it most likely to be?
options: Sphalerite, a zinc sulfide mineral
Chalcopyrite, a copper iron sulfide
Native gold, a soft and dense metal
Pyrite, a hard iron sulfide mineral
questions.explanation: Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) is brassy yellow with a greenish-black streak and is soft enough to scratch with a knife. Gold gives a yellow streak. Pyrite also has a dark streak but is harder than a steel knife, and sphalerite is usually brown with a pale streak.

questions.stem: Which property set identifies graphite?
options: Very dense, yellow streak, bends without breaking
Strongly magnetic, black streak, metallic lustre
Very soft, greasy feel, black streak that marks paper
Very hard, glassy lustre, white streak, no cleavage
questions.explanation: Graphite is pure carbon in sheets that slide over each other, so it is very soft, feels greasy and leaves a black mark, which is why it is used in pencils. A yellow streak and malleability describe gold; strong magnetism describes magnetite.

questions.stem: A dense, black, pitchy-looking mineral makes a Geiger counter click rapidly. Which ore mineral is it most likely to be?
options: Sphalerite, a sulfide of zinc
Bauxite, a hydroxide of aluminium
Uraninite, an oxide of uranium
Rutile, an oxide of titanium
questions.explanation: Uraninite (mainly UO2) is dense and black with a pitch-like lustre, and its radioactivity is a chemical property that identifies it. Rutile, sphalerite and bauxite are not radioactive.
